L01:
FlagShip raised a $4.2M seed round, led by Basis Ventures.

Eighteen months ago we started building a feature-flag platform on one belief: shipping software shouldn't be scary, and flags shouldn't be the thing you bolt on after your release process breaks. We're still 6 people. The belief hasn't changed.

The money buys two things: more engineers, and faster shipping for the early customers who bet on us before it was obvious.

We're hiring. If you build developer tools, my DMs are open.
L02:
Nine months, 3 teams, and the monolith is finally gone. This week we completed our migration to microservices at our fintech.

The numbers: p99 latency down 40%, deploys that took hours now take minutes, and 3 teams shipping independently without stepping on each other.

But the technical work was the easy part. The hard part was alignment — getting 3 teams to agree on service boundaries, ownership, and standards took more energy than any line of code.

Two things I'd tell anyone starting one of these: draw your boundaries from the domain, not the technology, and migrate incrementally, because big bangs fail.

Microservices get called overhyped, often fairly. For a fintech with 3 teams tripping over each other in one codebase, they were exactly the right tool.
L03:
We're hiring our first designer — a founding designer at our AI startup in Austin.

First design hire means you set the visual identity, the design culture, and the bar, with no legacy decisions to inherit. You report directly to the CEO. Equity is 0.5–1%: real ownership, not a courtesy grant.

The honest version of the job: no design system, no research backlog, no second designer to argue with. If that sounds like a problem, this isn't your role. If it sounds like the whole point, it is.

Austin preferred, flexible for the right person. DM me, or send this to the best designer you know.
L04:
In January I was laid off from a big tech company. Six months later, I've joined a 30-person startup to lead product.

The months in between were the hardest of my career. 200+ applications, and most of them disappeared into silence, which turned out to be worse than the rejections.

I won't dress it up as a growth story. It was a slog. The one thing I'd pass on: your job is not your identity — and it apparently takes losing one to believe that.

To the hiring managers who sent real rejections instead of nothing: it mattered.

If you're deep in a job search right now, my DMs are open.
L05:
Most AI agent startups are thin wrappers around the same 3 foundation models.

The pattern repeats every week: a clever prompt, a polished UI, and a foundation model doing all the actual work underneath. Prompts are not a moat. Anyone can copy one in an afternoon.

What is a moat: workflow depth and data. Embed deeply enough into how a team works that switching hurts, and build feedback loops that make the product smarter with every use. The best demo won't win this market; the company that understands its customers' workflows best will.

If you're building one, the only question worth asking: if the model providers ship your feature tomorrow, what's left?
L06:
Back from SaaStr Annual, where I talked with 40+ founders. Three things kept coming up.

PLG is maturing. It's no longer a buzzword or a religion — companies are getting genuinely sophisticated about layering sales on top of self-serve.

AI pricing is unsettled. Seat-based, usage-based, outcome-based: every founder I asked is experimenting, and not one sounded confident. That was the most interesting signal of the week.

Community-led growth is back, this time with ROI expectations attached. The version that was all vibes and no numbers didn't survive.

More energy in SaaS than I've seen in years.
L07:
Roughly 70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production, and the models are almost never the reason.

Two things kill them. Data readiness: you can't build production AI on fragmented, ungoverned data spread across spreadsheets and silos, and most enterprises are trying to. And missing process redesign: bolting AI onto an existing workflow and expecting magic. AI doesn't just automate a process — it demands you rethink it, and pilots that skip that step die at the demo.

The companies getting AI into production aren't the ones with the best models. They did the unglamorous work first: cleaned the data, redesigned the processes, prepared their people for the change. The model was the easy part.
L08:
Clearlens v2 is live.

Two new features, and they're the two that came up over and over across 300+ customer interviews: session replay, so you can watch exactly how users move through your product, and funnel comparison, so you can put two conversion funnels side by side and see which one is actually working.

We didn't guess at this roadmap. Customers told us what it should be, repeatedly — and 14 beta customers spent the past few months breaking early versions until they held up.

If you want to see what your users are really doing, the link is in the comments.
L09:
The most useful thing I've done in 10 years of B2B sales is shut up for 90 seconds.

The deal was falling apart on a call. The prospect had concerns, and every instinct said jump in with answers. I didn't. Ninety seconds of silence — excruciating — and then they talked themselves through their own objection and told me the real blocker, one I never would have guessed. We closed two weeks later.

A decade in, I'm convinced listening is the whole job. Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them if you can stand the pause long enough to let them.
L10:
After 3 years, I'm shutting down Cartful.

We raised $1.1M, grew to 4,000 users, and never found repeatable revenue. That last clause took me a long time to write, because for most of those years I let the user growth stand in for the answer.

Three lessons, at full price:

Users are not customers. We celebrated signups to avoid the harder question — who pays, and why.

One-off deals aren't traction. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one.

Runway is for learning, not surviving. We stretched ours to stay alive when we should have spent it finding the truth faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you, and I'm sorry we couldn't get there.
L11:
A few months ago I stopped daily standups for my team of 14. We replaced them with async written updates: each morning, everyone posts what they did, what they're doing, and what's blocking them.

Six hours of meetings gone per week. Shipping speed: unchanged. Engineers report fewer interruptions and more deep work, and time zones stopped mattering.

The uncomfortable conclusion: most standups aren't for the team, they're for the manager. A status ritual dressed up as collaboration. Written updates do the same job better — people think before they write, and the record is searchable.

Standups aren't always wrong. But if yours feels like a status meeting, it is one, and your team already knows.
L12:
I passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam.

Eleven weeks of studying around a full-time job, 5 practice exams, and the hardest certification I've attempted.

What actually worked: an hour every day instead of heroic Saturdays. Practice exams over rereading — each of the 5 exposed gaps I didn't know I had. Hands-on labs over videos, because nothing stuck until I built it. And treating the study hour like a meeting, since otherwise it's the first thing to go.

If you're doing this around a full-time job: it's a grind, but it's doable.
L13:
One year into engineering management, and the hardest part wasn't what I expected.

Not the meetings, not the 1:1s, not the difficult conversations. It was losing my scoreboard. For years, my sense of progress came from shipping — green squares, merged PRs, things I could point at. Then my output went invisible. A good week now means my 7 reports are unblocked, growing, and shipping while my own name appears nowhere, and it took months to stop feeling like an impostor about it.

Year one, distilled: the team's output is your output. Most problems are communication problems in disguise. Clarity is the most valuable thing you can hand anyone. And resisting the urge to jump in and fix it yourself is harder than it sounds.

If you're a new EM fighting the identity shift, it's not just you.
L14:
Our team of 9 SREs cut on-call pages 30% in one quarter. No new tooling, no re-architecture. We wrote runbooks.

The rules were simple: every incident gets a runbook entry, every repeated page triggers a documentation review, outdated docs get deleted as aggressively as new ones get written, and runbook quality counts toward done.

Pages dropped not because the systems got better, but because the knowledge stopped living only in people's heads.

Nobody gets promoted for writing runbooks, which is exactly why they're underpriced. If your team is drowning in pages, the fix probably isn't another tool. It's writing down what the person who always gets paged already knows.
L15:
After 3 years fully remote, we went hybrid: 2 days in the office. The honest scorecard.

The good: retention is the best it's been in two years, onboarding is noticeably faster, and cross-team collaboration is easier.

The cost: 2 senior people quit over the change. Trust took a hit during the transition. And some days the office is half empty, and the people who commuted are right to wonder why.

I no longer believe there's a correct answer to remote vs hybrid. Every model has tradeoffs; every policy disappoints someone. What you owe your team is the real reason for the change, and respect for the people who make a different call — two of ours did, and I respect them for it.

Anyone claiming this is a solved problem is selling something.
L16:
AI won't replace junior developers, but it's rewriting what "junior" means.

We recently hired 2 junior engineers. Both use AI pair-programming tools daily, and both ship production code faster than juniors did five years ago — not slightly faster, a lot. What's changed is where their value sits: less memorized syntax and boilerplate, more critical code review, better questions, systems thinking from day one.

The implications are bigger than they look. Hiring rubrics built on syntax trivia are obsolete. Mentorship matters more, not less, because judgment doesn't autocomplete. And the ladder from junior to senior is compressing.

Which is why "we stopped hiring juniors because AI" is a strategic mistake, not a cost saving. You're not cutting a line item. You're cutting your future senior pipeline.
L17:
A churned customer came back last week, unprompted.

When they left, they told us plainly: our seat-based pricing punished them for growing, and they were paying for licenses nobody used. So we switched to usage-based. It was scary — we modeled the downside a dozen times, and some advisors told us not to do it.

Since the switch: expansion revenue is up 22%, sales conversations start with value instead of license counts, and — the part I didn't expect — churned customers are returning on their own.

Pricing is a statement about whose side you're on. Seat-based rewarded us when customers overbought. Usage-based only pays us when they succeed. Aligning those incentives turned out to be good business, not just good ethics.
L18:
Six months ago, a bootcamp grad asked me to mentor them. This week they signed an offer as a frontend developer at an insurance company.

The hard work was theirs. What we did together was unglamorous: weekly check-ins even when progress felt slow, code reviews on real projects instead of toy exercises, 4 mock interviews that got harder each round, and honest conversations about rejection.

What I learned: mentorship isn't having all the answers. It's showing up consistently while someone's confidence wobbles.

The industry loves debating whether bootcamp grads can make it. This one did, with grit and about an hour of my week — the cheapest career-changing thing an experienced developer can give.

To my mentee: congratulations. You earned every bit of it.
L19:
We changed one email subject line and open rates jumped 31%.

For months, sends to our 18k subscribers led with features: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." Fine open rates, nothing special. Then we rewrote one to lead with the outcome instead. Same email, same list, same send time.

Feature-focused: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard"
Outcome-focused: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking"

One talks about us. The other talks about the reader. Up 31%.

The lesson is as old as marketing and we still needed the reminder: customers don't care what you built, they care what it does for them. We've since rewritten every lifecycle subject line the same way, and the gains have held.

Audit your last 10 subject lines. Count how many are about you.
L20:
Our 12-person company runs on 5 tools.

Linear, for every task, bug, and project — if it's not there, it doesn't exist. Notion, as the company brain. Slack, with strict channel hygiene. Figma, where product ideas get real before any code is written. And Otto, our homegrown deploy bot: one command takes code from PR to production. Everyone's favorite teammate.

That's the whole stack. No overlapping subscriptions, no "which doc is the source of truth."

The principle: every tool is a tax — context-switching, licenses, onboarding, integrations. We add one only when the pain of not having it beats the tax. So far, five is enough.
L21:
I just took my first real break in 4 years. Two weeks, no Slack, no email.

The first days were uncomfortable — checking my phone out of habit, guilt, the conviction things would fall apart without me. They didn't.

The useful part came after. Looking at my calendar with two weeks of distance, I could see how much of my busyness was self-inflicted. In my first week back I killed 3 recurring meetings. Nobody has missed them.

Two things I now believe: if your business can't survive two weeks without you, that's a design flaw, not a badge of honor. And rest isn't a reward for finishing the work, because the work is never finished.

The sabbatical you think you can't afford is probably the one you need.
L22:
Three years ago we were 4 people in a garage in Denver — folding tables, a space heater, a whiteboard off Craigslist. This week we hired employee #50.

We serve 900 customers now, and the thing I'm proudest of isn't the growth. It's that the values we scribbled on that whiteboard still hold: customers first, default to transparency, hire people better than yourself. Fifty people in, they've survived contact with reality.

To the first 4: thank you for believing when there was nothing to believe in. To the newest 46: thank you for choosing us.

Back to work.
L23:
My last 3 clients all came from writing online. From years of conferences, mixers, and founder happy hours — hundreds of business cards collected — zero.

Writing wins on three axes. Scale: a conversation reaches one person, a post reaches thousands. Selection: the right people come to you already sold on how you think. Compounding: a good post keeps working for months, while a handshake is forgotten by Monday.

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

Relationships still matter — they're everything. But the best ones now start when someone reads your ideas and thinks "this person gets it," not when you trade business cards.

Stop collecting contacts. Publish your thinking.
L24:
I joined Supply Chain Weekly for episode 142 to talk about AI demand forecasting.

The number I keep coming back to: at one of our pilot customers, forecast error is down 18%. That isn't an abstract metric. It means less overstock, fewer stockouts, and real working capital freed up.

We also got into why traditional forecasting breaks down in volatile markets, what AI-driven forecasting actually looks like past the buzzwords, and the hard parts nobody leads with — data quality, change management, and why the forecasting team's expertise matters more with AI, not less.

Thanks to the hosts for asking real questions. If you work in supply chain, operations, or planning, the episode link is in the comments.
L25:
Year in review: ARR went from $1.2M to $3.4M, the team from 9 to 21, and NPS sits at 61.

Best year in the company's history by almost every measure — and the number I care about most is the NPS, because growth on top of customers who don't love the product is borrowed time.

Now the part these posts usually skip. My biggest mistake: hiring sales too early. We brought on reps before we, the founders, had nailed the sales motion ourselves. Months of missed targets and frustrated reps followed, and it wasn't their fault — you can't hand off a playbook you haven't written. We rebuilt the process from first principles and it finally clicked, but I'd take those months back if I could.

Growth is messy. The highlight reel just edits it out.
